What Comes After AGI?
entry.content:
What comes after AGI?

As multiple technological routes toward artificial general superintelligence take shape, the regime beyond AGI is shifting from philosophical speculation to empirical research and governance questions.

For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.

Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.

The continuum of general intelligence

To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.

ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades).

Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.

Yet knowing those upper limits doesnât tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, itâs hard to predict how capable a âgood enoughâ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.

What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both todayâs AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted.

Cognitive industrialization

Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient.

Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute, driven by three compounding factors:

Hardware manufacturing improvements: Under Moore's law and related trends, compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades - meaning the same investment 18 months from now buys twice the compute. Algorithmic efficiency: The amount of training compute (FLOPs) required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3â6x per year over the last decade, while algorithmic efficiency at inference improved by roughly 3x per year. Doubling efficiency is practically equivalent to doubling the stock of physical compute. Compute hardware investment: Spending on AI hardware has grown by roughly 2.5x per year over the past decade. For example, the training compute of the largest frontier training runs grows by more than 4x per year.

Multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world.

At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year. A cognitive workload that can be performed by todayâs AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023.

Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised. Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services.

Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? Itâs certainly not a given, but practical ceilings on compute build-out, and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of todayâs AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now.

Would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up todayâs AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own. Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI.

Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways:

Processing speed: AI systems can reason, ingest data, and generate outputs at increasingly high rates. Working memory and memorization: Todayâs models can literally memorize large parts of the internet and their working memory capacity far exceeds human limits. Substrate independence: The same AI system can migrate from one computer to another, upgrade to faster or more energy-efficient hardware, or run across heterogeneous, spatially distributed fleets. Lossless replication: Digital intelligence can be copied nearly instantly and without loss - not only its source code (akin to DNA), but also its memory state (our lifetime experience). Specialist systems can be trained once, then spawned in millions of copies when needed. High-bandwidth sharing of experiences: Humans must strongly compress experience and knowledge in order to teach others; AIs can replay stored high-bandwidth digital input-output streams across an entire population, and homogeneous AI groups could share raw learning signals directly. Four pathways from AGI to ASI

Dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level. But some missing capabilities may be hard - or impossible - to patch over with sheer volume. While Einstein did figure out general relativity, a conference of one hundred thousand Ptolemaic astronomers probably wouldnât have.

AI could follow four potential technological pathways to unlock previously unavailable cognitive capabilities. (For an in-depth discussion, see our From AGI to ASI report.)

Scaling models and data

So far, qualitative capabilities have improved with remarkable consistency alongside model and data scale. This trend is captured by scaling laws that relate model performance to training compute, training data, and more recently, test-time compute (giving a model extra computing power to reason through a problem before answering).

These scaling âlaws,â however, are extrapolations of observed trends that hold only within familiar boundaries, such as a particular model architecture, type of training data, and family of evaluations. They canât confidently predict the scale required for AGI or ASI, but we can identify potential bottlenecks to continued scaling of models and data:

Data exhaustion: The need for larger amounts of high-quality training data is outpacing humanityâs ability to produce more of it. âSyntheticâ data could help, but not all data produced by AI models is useful for training. To overcome this âdata wall,â researchers could rely on high-fidelity simulations, generate data within interactive (RL) environments, and use test-time compute to create better training data for future AI models. Diminishing returns on model scale: Each linear step up in model capability typically requires multiplying, not just adding, training compute and model size - but bigger models are slower, thus bottlenecking test-time scaling methods such as chain-of-thought reasoning. Physical and economic resource limits: Sustaining multi-order-of-magnitude increases in training compute runs up against real-world limits in building power plants, electrical grids, chip fabrication plants, and low-latency hardware interconnects. It remains unclear whether hardware and software efficiency gains - the main trends underlying cognitive industrialization - can compensate for this. Technological paradigm shifts

Todayâs dominant AI paradigm is to train large transformers to predict the next symbol in a long sequence across vast datasets, then refine them to learn to reason and follow instructions, and give them extra test-time compute. Recent research suggests this paradigm can, in principle, produce models that can run complex algorithms, including powerful learning algorithms, via their prompts - that is, without requiring retraining. This is a key ingredient for building AI systems at the theoretical upper limit of intelligence.

But todayâs models fall short of humans on a few fundamental dimensions, including continual learning, certain forms of world modeling, decision-making, and sample efficiency - meaning that AI models need to be initially trained on much more data than humans to reach roughly the same intelligence level. They may also be missing the ability to invent genuinely new concepts and abstractions rather than recombining existing ones. Researchers are divided on whether these problems can be solved with simple extensions and evolutions of todayâs paradigm, or whether reaching ASI will require truly deep technological paradigm shifts.

Improving agent coordination

Human corporations, markets, and research communities solve problems that no individual could tackle alone. Similarly, coordinating thousands or millions of AGI instances into "group agents" or virtual agent economies could produce collective superintelligence. What is unclear today is how AI group intelligence could scale as we add more agents and compute, depending on how agents are organized. That is, we need multi-agent scaling laws. Early research finds clear intelligence gains in some tasks, but coordination inefficiencies still lead to diminishing returns as the population size grows.

Less obviously, steering large agent collectives will require robust institutional design and organizational mechanisms, including defenses against accidental or intentional misinformation spread, manipulation, and collusion. Experiments with agent swarms are already demonstrating how quickly these dynamics can emerge, with individual agents learning to cheat and others acting as whistleblowers to expose them.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI)

Finally, AI systems could begin automating improvements to future generations of AI - a process known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) that was first discussed by I. J. Good and Ray Solomonoff.

Unlike typical technological development, improvements to AI could directly speed up subsequent gains, leading to an accelerating rate of progress. However, further improvements in research tend to be âharder to findâ - more and more effort is required to maintain the same rate of improvement across technologies. Whether RSI leads to ârunawayâ progress is largely an empirical question.

RSI is not a single process. It can operate via improvements to code and designs - from model architectures and training algorithms to chip layouts. It can also operate through data, by spending compute at deployment to produce improved results and outputs that can be reused to train future models. AlphaZero self-improved purely in this data driven way to reach superhuman performance.

Finally, RSI can play out at the group level by dividing labor and specializing roles in an agent collective. A group of coordinated specialists can achieve more than the sum of what they could achieve as isolated generalists, in turn becoming more effective at finding further improvements. Instead of just scaling up a team with fixed roles, larger and more efficient collectives enable new types of specialization that were previously unviable - much like how a multi-cellular organism can support specialized organs like a heart or a brain, as opposed to a single-celled organism that perform all survival functions on its own.

These three RSI mechanisms mirror evolutionary processes that drove the growth of human cognitive capabilities: genetic (code and design), cultural (data), and social evolution (group specialization through cooperation).

Importantly, RSI loops can easily stall or degenerate if the feedback guiding them is poor. Pursuing ASI via recursive self-improvement therefore requires evaluation methods that can be rapidly scaled into the superhuman regime, where even large groups of humans can't easily assess AI outputs. Accordingly, RSI should advance fastest in domains that allow for automated verification without humans in the loop, such as mathematical proofs, while other domains might lag behind or taper off sooner.

The many roads to ASI

These pathways to ASI are not mutually exclusive - in fact, they compound on one another. If progress on one stalls, economic and geopolitical competition will likely shift effort toward the others. Even if RSI doesnât result in runaway gains, continued scaling in training data, speed, efficiency, and coordination could still drive rapid progress well beyond human-level AGI

Because there are multiple routes to superintelligence, trying to slow down AI development by restricting just one area - like the computing power for training an AI model - won't be enough to stop overall progress. Equally, suppressing a single dimension risks creating a capability âoverhangâ: if multiple inputs need to be combined to make progress, holding back one dimension while the others move forward would lead to sudden, steep jumps in progress when the suppressed dimension is relaxed (or overcome otherwise).

Taking all these arguments together, continued fast AI progress over the next decade is a serious possibility. It could take us relatively smoothly from today, to Expert AGI, and then into the superhuman AI regime, accelerating science and enabling breakthroughs in fields like medicine, materials, and clean energy. Even in the absence of dramatic frontier AI progress, cognitive industrialization alone could reshape knowledge work and the broader economy. Regardless of which path AI progress takes, we must anticipate far-reaching opportunities along with equally transformative pressures to many aspects of human society.

None of these predictions are certain, but the pathways and scenarios are also far from unfounded hype or fiction. So what can be done? Our best course of action may sound familiar: model, measure, forecast, and repeat. While those steps arenât surprising, the complexity and scale of carrying them out on the road to ASI is entirely unprecedented. It requires large-scale and highly-interdisciplinary efforts across both frontier labs and national and global institutions. Many of the key metrics for tracking progress on these pathways require frontier-model access and sizable amounts of evaluation compute, alongside new benchmarking and modelling methodologies that could spawn entirely new research fields.

Human-level AGI has long been the horizon for AI research, but it is far from the upper limit of intelligence. Understanding what could come next - and its implications across science, industry, and society - is the grand challenge ahead for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

Acknowledgements

This essay is based on the technical report From AGI to ASI, co-authored with Matija Franklin, Alexander Lerchner, Laurent Orseau, Samuel Albanie, Adam Bales, Cole Wyeth, Stephanie Chan, Iason Gabriel, Joel Z. Leibo, Allan Dafoe, Marcus Hutter, Thore Graepel, and Shane Legg, as well as subsequent discussions within the DeepMind Institute team. Thanks also to Nenad TomaÅ¡ev, Seb Krier, Davide Paglieri, Sasha Vezhnevets, Alison Snyder, and Fin Moorhouse for helpful discussions and feedback.

entry.title: PostgreSQL 19
entry.content:
Release date: 2026-11-19

PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including:

New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table.

pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query.

Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations.

Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica.

Logical replication of sequence values.

Support for “read-your-writes” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command.

Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system.

The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below.

A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases.

Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities:

Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) §

The default warning period is seven days.

Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) §

The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings. MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18.

Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) §

PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP, which is unfixably insecure.

Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) §

Dumps created using pre-PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall, and using standard_conforming_strings = off, will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on.

Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off, for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary.

Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) §

pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems.

Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § §

The btree_gist inet/cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet/cidr indexes.

Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) §

The values of such columns were not well-defined.

Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) §

This previously returned NULL.

Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) §

This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions.

Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) §

Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases.

Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) §

This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2.

Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §

Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT.

Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §

Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit. With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.

Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) §

This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.

Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) §

Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared, BufferShareExclusive, and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) §

Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) §

Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) §

Change psql's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) §

Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) §

Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU, builtin) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C, the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values.

Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non-ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § §

dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex(), metaphone(), and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade.

Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) §

This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding.

Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release.

Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOINs when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) §

Allow more LEFT JOINs to be converted to ANTI JOINs (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) §

Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOINs with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) §

Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § §

This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed.

Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) §

Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) §

Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) §

Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) §

The latter form is more easily optimized.

Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) §

Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) §

This allows for later optimizations.

Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § §

Simplify IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to plain boolean expressions when the input is proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) §

Speed up join selectivity computations for large optimizer statistics targets (Ilia Evdokimov, David Geier) §

Add proper optimizer statistics for functions returning boolean values (Tom Lane) §

Allow extended statistics on virtual generated columns (Yugo Nagata) §

Allow function pg_restore_extended_stats() to restore optimizer extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier, Chao Li) § § § §

Add function pg_clear_extended_stats() to remove extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) §

Adjust the optimizer to consider startup costs of partial paths (Robert Haas, Tomas Vondra) §

Allow negative values of pg_aggregate.aggtransspace to indicate unbounded memory usage (Richard Guo) §

This information is used by the optimizer in planning memory usage.

Improve performance of foreign key constraint checks (Junwang Zhao, Amit Langote, Chao Li) § §

Improve asynchronous I/O read-ahead scheduling for large requests (Andres Freund) § § §

Allow io_method method worker to automatically control needed background workers (Thomas Munro) §

The new server variables are io_min_workers, io_max_workers, io_worker_idle_timeout, and io_worker_launch_interval.

Allow query table scans to mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map (Melanie Plageman) §

Previously only VACUUM and COPY ... FREEZE could do this.

Allow autovacuum to use parallel autovacuum workers (Daniil Davydov) § §

The maximum number of workers is controlled by server variable autovacuum_max_parallel_workers and per-table storage parameter autovacuum_parallel_workers.

Allow TID Range Scans to be parallelized (Cary Huang, David Rowley) §

Improve COPY FROM performance for text and CSV input using SIMD CPU instructions (Nazir Bilal Yavuz, Shinya Kato) §

Improve NOTIFY to only wake up backends that are listening to specified notifications (Joel Jacobson) §

Previously most backends were woken by NOTIFY.

Change wal_compression equals on to use the best WAL compression method available (wenhui qiu) §

Previously this always used pglz.

Change the default TOAST compression method from pglz to the more efficient lz4 (Euler Taveira) §

This is done by changing the default for server variable default_toast_compression.

Improve performance of internal row deformation (David Rowley) §

Improve performance of repeated UTF-8 case-folding operations (Andreas Karlsson) §

Improve performance of hash index bulk-deletion and GIN index vacuuming using streaming reads (Xuneng Zhou) § §

Improve sort performance using radix sort (John Naylor) §

Improve timing performance measurements (Lukas Fittl, Andres Freund, David Geier) § §

This benefits EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING) and pg_test_timing, and is controlled via server variable timing_clock_source.

Optimize plpgsql syntax SELECT simple-expression INTO var (Tom Lane) §

Add system view pg_stat_lock and function pg_stat_get_lock() to report per-lock-type statistics (Bertrand Drouvot) §

Add system view pg_stat_recovery to report recovery status (Xuneng Zhou, Shinya Kato) § §

Add system view pg_stat_progress_repack to report the progress of REPACK, CLUSTER, and VACUUM FULL (Álvaro Herrera) §

Add system view pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to report per-table autovacuum details (Sami Imseih) §

Add vacuum initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_vacuum (Shinya Kato) §

The new started_by column reports the initiator of the vacuum, and mode indicates its aggressiveness.

Add analyze initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_analyze (Shinya Kato) §

The new started_by column reports the initiator of the analyze.

Add system view pg_dsm_registry_allocations to report dynamic shared memory details (Florents Tselai, Nathan Bossart) § §

Add mem_exceeded_count column to system view pg_stat_replication_slots (Bertrand Drouvot) §

This reports the number of times that logical_decoding_work_mem was exceeded.

Add slot synchronization skip information to pg_stat_replication_slots and pg_replication_slots (Shlok Kyal) § § §

The new columns are slotsync_skip_count, slotsync_last_skip, and slotsync_skip_reason.

Add update_deleted column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Zhijie Hou) §

This reports the number of rows where updates were ignored due to concurrent deletes. This requires the subscriber have retain_dead_tuples enabled.

Add sync_seq_error_count column to system view pg_stat_subscription_stats to report sequence synchronization errors (Vignesh C) § §

Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_all_tables, pg_stat_all_indexes, and pg_statio_all_sequences (Bertrand Drouvot, Sami Imseih, Shihao Zhong) §

It also appears in the sys and user view variants.

Add stats_reset column to system views pg_stat_user_functions and pg_stat_database_conflicts (Bertrand Drouvot, Shihao Zhong) § §

Add location column to system views pg_available_extensions and pg_available_extension_versions to report the file system directory of extensions (Matheus Alcantara) §

Add backup_type column to system view pg_stat_progress_basebackup to report the type of backup (Shinya Kato) §

Possible values are full or incremental.

Add connecting value to system view column pg_stat_wal_receiver.status (Xuneng Zhou) §

Add reporting of the bytes written to WAL for full page images (Shinya Kato) §

This is accessible via system view pg_stat_wal and function pg_stat_get_backend_wal().

Add columns to system views pg_stats, pg_stats_ext, and pg_stats_ext_exprs (Corey Huinker) §

Adds table OID and attribute number columns to pg_stats, and table OID and statistics object OID columns to the other two.

Add information about range type extended statistics to system view pg_stats_ext_exprs (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) §

Allow log_min_messages log levels to be specified by process type (Euler Taveira) §

The new format is type:level. A value without a colon controls all process types, allowing backward compatibility.

Add server variable log_autoanalyze_min_duration to log long-running analyze operations by autovacuum operations (Shinya Kato) §

Server variable log_autovacuum_min_duration now only controls logging of vacuum operations by autovacuum.

Enable server variable log_lock_waits by default (Laurenz Albe) §

Add server variable debug_print_raw_parse to log raw parse trees (Chao Li) §

This is also enabled when the server is started with debug level three and higher.

Make messages coming from remote servers appear in the server logs in the same format as local server messages (Vignesh C) §

These include replication, postgres_fdw, and dblink servers.

Add reporting of WAL full-page write bytes to VACUUM and ANALYZE logging (Shinya Kato) §

Add IO wait events for COPY FROM/TO on a pipe, file, or program (Nikolay Samokhvalov) §

Add wait events for commit_delay and for WAL write and flush LSNs (Xuneng Zhou) § §

Have pg_get_sequence_data() return the sequence page LSN (Vignesh C) §

Add function pg_get_multixact_stats() to report multixact activity (Naga Appani) §

Issue warnings when the wraparound of transaction IDs or multixacts is less than 100 million away (Nathan Bossart) §

The previous warning was 40 million. Warnings are issued to clients and in the server log.

Add scoring system to control the order that tables are processed by autovacuum (Nathan Bossart) §

The new server variables are autovacuum_freeze_score_weight, autovacuum_multixact_freeze_score_weight, autovacuum_vacuum_score_weight, autovacuum_vacuum_insert_score_weight, and autovacuum_analyze_score_weight.

Add server-side support for SNI (Server Name Indication) (Daniel Gustafsson, Jacob Champion) §

New configuration file PGDATA/pg_hosts.conf specifies hostname/key pairs.

Allow OAuth validators to register custom pg_hba.conf authentication options (Jacob Champion, Zsolt Parragi) §

Allow roles pg_read_all_data and pg_write_all_data to read/write large objects (Nitin Motiani, Nathan Bossart) §

These roles are designed to allow non-super users to run pg_dump.

Allow background workers to be configured to terminate before database-level operations (Aya Iwata) §

This allows database-level operations to complete more quickly since blocking background workers can now be terminated.

Allow server variables that represent lists to be emptied by setting the value to NULL (Tom Lane) §

Update GB18030 encoding from version 2000 to 2022 (Chao Li, Zheng Tao) §

See the commit message for compatibility details.

Add WAIT command to allow standbys to wait for LSN values to be written, flushed, or replayed (Kartyshov Ivan, Alexander Korotkov, Xuneng Zhou) § §

Improve function pg_sync_replication_slots() to wait for replication synchronization completion (Ajin Cherian, Zhijie Hou) §

Previously, certain synchronization failures would not be reported.

Add server variable wal_sender_shutdown_timeout to limit replica synchronization waits during shutdown (Andrey Silitskiy, Hayato Kuroda) §

By default, senders still wait forever for synchronization.

Allow sequence values stored in subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) § § §

This occurs during ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... [ADD|SET|REFRESH|DROP] PUBLICATION. Function pg_get_sequence_data() allows inspection of sequence synchronization.

Allow CREATE/ALTER PUBLICATION to publish all sequences (Vignesh C, Tomas Vondra) §

This is enabled with the ALL SEQUENCES clause.

Allow ALTER SUBSCRIPTION on publications to synchronize the existence of sequences on subscribers to match the publisher (Vignesh C) §

This is enabled with the REFRESH SEQUENCES clause.

Allow CREATE/ALTER PUBLICATION to exclude some tables (Vignesh C, Shlok Kyal) § § § §

This is controlled with the EXCEPT clause, and is useful when specifying ALL TABLES.

Add CREATE/ALTER SUBSCRIPTION setting retain_dead_tuples to retain information needed for conflict detection (Zhijie Hou) § § §

Also add setting max_retention_duration to limit retain_dead_tuples retention.

Allow CREATE SUBSCRIPTION to use postgres_fdw foreign data wrapper connection parameters (Jeff Davis) §

The connection parameters are referenced via CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER.

When server variable wal_level is replica, allow automatic enablement of logical replication when needed (Masahiko Sawada) §

New server variable effective_wal_level, application pg_controldata, and function pg_control_checkpoint() report the effective WAL level.

Allow wal_receiver_timeout to be set per-subscription and user (Fujii Masao) § §

This allows subscribers to use different wal_receiver_timeout values.

Add optional pid parameter to pg_replication_origin_session_setup() to allow parallelization of SQL-level replication solutions (Doruk Yilmaz, Hayato Kuroda) §

Allow GROUP BY to process target list subqueries that have expressions referencing non-subquery columns (Tom Lane) §

Also fix a bug in how GROUPING() handles target list subquery aliases.

Allow window functions to ignore NULLs with the IGNORE NULLS/RESPECT NULLS clause (Oliver Ford, Tatsuo Ishii) §

Supported window functions are lead(), lag(), first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value().

Add support for INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING (Andreas Karlsson, Marko Tiikkaja, Viktor Holmberg) §

This allows conflicting rows to be returned, and optionally locked with FOR UPDATE/SHARE.

Add REPACK command which replaces VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER (Antonin Houska) §

The two former commands did similar things, but with confusing names, so unify them as REPACK. The old commands have been retained for compatibility.

Allow REPACK to rebuild tables without access-exclusive locking (Antonin Houska, Mihail Nikalayeu, Álvaro Herrera) § § §

This is enabled via the CONCURRENTLY option. Server variable max_repack_replication_slots was also added.

Allow GRANT/REVOKE to specify the effective role performing the privileges adjustment (Nathan Bossart, Tom Lane) §

The GRANTED BY clause controls this.

Support forward references in FOREIGN KEY constraint clauses within CREATE SCHEMA (Jian He, Tom Lane) §

Allow CHECKPOINT to accept a list of options (Christoph Berg) § § §

Supported options are MODE and FLUSH_UNLOGGED.

Add CONNECTION clause to CREATE FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER to specify a function to be called for subscription connection parameters (Jeff Davis, Noriyoshi Shinoda) § §

Add SUPPORT clause to CREATE AGGREGATE so extensions can specify support functions to optimize aggregate calls (Tom Lane) §

Add memory usage and parallelism reporting to VACUUM (VERBOSE) and autovacuum logs (Tatsuya Kawata, Daniil Davydov) § §

Allow ALTER TABLE ALTER CONSTRAINT ... [NOT] ENFORCED for CHECK constraints (Jian He) §

Previously enforcement changes were only supported for foreign key constraints.

Allow ALTER TABLE ... COLUMN SET EXPRESSION to succeed on virtual columns with CHECK constraints (Jian He) §

This was previously prohibited.

Allow multiple headers lines to be skipped by COPY FROM (Shinya Kato, Fujii Masao) §

Previously only a single header line could be skipped.

Allow COPY FROM to set invalid input values to NULL (Jian He, Kirill Reshke) §

This is done using the COPY option ON_ERROR SET_NULL.

Allow COPY TO to output JSON format (Joe Conway, Jian He, Andrew Dunstan) § §

JSON output can also be a single JSON array using the COPY option FORCE_ARRAY.

Allow COPY TO to process partitioned tables (Jian He, Ajin Cherian) § §

Previously COPY (SELECT ...) had to be used to output partitioned tables. This also improves logical replication table synchronization.

Add EXPLAIN ANALYZE option IO to report asynchronous IO activity (Tomas Vondra) § § §

Add reporting of WAL full-page write bytes to EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL) output (Shinya Kato) §

Add Memoize cache and lookup estimates to EXPLAIN output (Ilia Evdokimov, Lukas Fittl) §

This can show why Memoize was chosen.

Add the 64-bit unsigned data type oid8 (Michael Paquier) §

Add more jsonpath string methods (Florents Tselai, David E. Wheeler) §

They are ltrim(), rtrim(), btrim(), lower(), upper(), initcap(), replace(), and split_part(). These are immutable like their non-JSON string variants.

Allow casts between bytea and uuid data types (Dagfinn Ilmari Mannsåker, Aleksander Alekseev) §

Add ability to cast between database names and oids using regdatabase (Ian Lawrence Barwick) §

Add functions tid_block() and tid_offset() to extract block numbers and offsets from tid values (Ayush Tiwari) §

Add date, timestamp, and timestamptz versions of random(min, max) (Damien Clochard, Dean Rasheed) § §

Allow encode() and decode() to process data in base64url and base32hex formats (Andrey Borodin, Aleksander Alekseev, Florents Tselai) § § §

This format retains ordering, unlike base32.

Add functions to return a set of ranges resulting from range subtraction (Paul A. Jungwirth) §

The functions are range_minus_multi() and multirange_minus_multi(). This is useful to represent range subtraction results with gaps.

Add function error_on_null() to return the supplied parameter, or error on NULL input (Joel Jacobson) §

Allow IS JSON to work on domains defined over supported base types (Jian He) §

The supported base types are TEXT, JSON, JSONB, and BYTEA.

Add full text stemmers for Polish and Esperanto (Tom Lane) §

The Dutch stemmer now uses a different algorithm, which changes the stems of many words; the previous algorithm is available via dutch_porter.

The English, French, German, Lithuanian, Norwegian, Spanish, Swedish, and Turkish stemmers have also been updated and produce different stems for some words.

Allow event triggers to be written using PL/Python (Euler Taveira, Dimitri Fontaine) §

Add special libpq protocol parameters for compatibility testing (Jelte Fennema-Nio, Jacob Champion) §

Otherwise known as protocol grease, which was active during the 19 beta period. These will no longer be sent as of the PostgreSQL 19 official release, but the parameter reservations will remain for potential use in the future.

Add libpq connection parameter oauth_ca_file to specify an alternate certificate authority when communicating with OAuth providers (Jonathan Gonzalez V., Jacob Champion) §

This can also be set via the PGOAUTHCAFILE environment variable. The default is to use curl's built-in certificates.

Allow libpq environment variable PGOAUTHDEBUG to specify particular debug options (Zsolt Parragi, Jacob Champion) §

The UNSAFE option still generates all debugging output.

Improve custom OAuth client flows (Jacob Champion) § §

Previously, libpq reported only a generic error message during custom flow failures, and each flow implementation was required to calculate the issuer identifier independently. Add a new authdata hook type PQAUTHDATA_OAUTH_BEARER_TOKEN_V2 that precomputes the issuer ID and lets hooks provide error details.

Add libpq function PQgetThreadLock() to retrieve the current locking callback (Jacob Champion) §

Allow the search path to appear in the psql prompt via %S (Florents Tselai) §

This works when psql is connected to PostgreSQL 18 or later.

Allow the hot standby status to appear in the psql prompt via %i (Jim Jones) §

Modify psql backslash commands to show comments for publications, subscriptions, and extended statistics (Fujii Masao, Jim Jones) §

The modified commands are \dRp+, \dRs+, and \dX+.

Allow control over how booleans are displayed in psql (David G. Johnston) §

The \pset variables are display_true and display_false.

Allow psql to more accurately determine if the pager is needed (Erik Wienhold) §

Add or improve psql tab completion (Yamaguchi Atsuo, Yugo Nagata, Haruna Miwa, Xuneng Zhou, Dagfinn Ilmari Mannsåker, Fujii Masao, Álvaro Herrera, Jian He, Tatsuya Kawata, Ian Lawrence Barwick, Vasuki M) § § § § § § § § § § § § § §

Allow pg_dump to include restorable extended statistics (Corey Huinker) §

Change vacuumdb's --analyze-only and --analyze-in-stages options to analyze partitioned tables when no targets are specified (Laurenz Albe, Mircea Cadariu, Chao Li) § §

Previously it skipped partitioned tables. This now matches the behavior of ANALYZE.

Allow vacuumdb to report its commands without running them using option --dry-run (Corey Huinker) §

Allow pg_verifybackup to read WAL files stored in tar archives (Amul Sul) §

Add option --wal-path as an alias for the existing and deprecated --wal-directory option.

Allow pg_waldump to read WAL files stored in tar archives (Amul Sul) §

Improve performance of pg_upgrade copying large object metadata (Nathan Bossart) § § § §

Various methods are used, depending on the PostgreSQL version of the old cluster.

Allow pg_upgrade to process non-default tablespaces stored in the PGDATA directory (Nathan Bossart) §

Previously such tablespaces generated an error.

Add pgbench option --continue-on-error to continue after SQL errors (Rintaro Ikeda, Yugo Nagata, Fujii Masao) §

Improve the usability of pg_test_timing (Hannu Krosing, Tom Lane) § §

Report nanoseconds instead of microseconds. In addition to histogram output, output a second table that reports exact timings, with an optional cutoff set by --cutoff.

If you find FFmpeg useful, you are welcome to contribute by donating. More downloading options Get packages & executable files

FFmpeg only provides source code. Below are some links that provide it already compiled and ready to go.

Linux Packages Linux Static Builds Windows EXE Files Get the Sources

You can retrieve the source code through Git by using the command:

git clone https://git.ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg.git ffmpeg

FFmpeg has always been a very experimental and developer-driven project. It is a key component in many multimedia projects and has new features added constantly. Development branch snapshots work really well 99% of the time so people are not afraid to use them.

Git Repositories

Since FFmpeg is developed with Git, multiple repositories from developers and groups of developers are available.

Clone URL Description Main FFmpeg Git repository https://git.ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-web Main ffmpeg.org website repository https://git.ffmpeg.org/fateserver fate.ffmpeg.org server software repository Mirrors Mirror of the main repository Mirror of the website repository Mirror of the FATE server repository
Release Verification

All FFmpeg releases are cryptographically signed with our public PGP key and should be verified for authenticity.

pub rsa2048 2011-04-26 [SC] FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8 uid [ full ] FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org> sub rsa2048 2011-04-26 [E]

To verify a release:

Import our public key into your local keyring: $ curl https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-devel.asc | gpg --import Download a release tarball and its corresponding signature. Verify the signature: $ gpg --verify ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz.asc ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz gpg: Signature made Sun 21 Feb 2021 06:35:15 AEST gpg: using RSA key FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8 gpg: issuer "ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org" gpg: Good signature from "FFmpeg release signing key <ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org>" [full]

Optionally, you can verify that git and tarball match, the only differences should be the absence of .git* files in the tarball and a VERSION file in the tarball containing the version. The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64

A release that also has a .pq.asc file carries post-quantum signatures (RFC 9980) made with both of these keys:

ML-DSA-87+Ed448 99669C49693683D51F174FE0D9E84915F5C2A536F5C0DA70FB8DCBD8AA8C4B3D SLH-DSA-256s 547721479F80449E77748C0235116A1F8A73D9ECA98673B90E4E39347D229989

GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed:

$ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz $ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz Releases

Approximately every 6 months the FFmpeg project makes a new major release. Between major releases point releases will appear that add important bug fixes but no new features. Note that these releases are intended for distributors and system integrators. Users that wish to compile from source themselves are strongly encouraged to consider using the development branch (see above), this is the only version on which FFmpeg developers actively work. The release branches only cherry pick selected changes from the development branch, which therefore receives much more and much faster bug fixes such as additional features and security patches.

entry.title: Jujutsu Primer
entry.content:
Why try Jujutsu?

jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Installing jj

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:

# macOS # Arch Linux # NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable) # From source # (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH) Setup and configuration

In an existing git repository, run:

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:

In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:

Commits and changes

A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

$ @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 849165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

The IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

$ Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb Change ID: royxmykxtrkrqppotnrvutxlvrvqyxmy Bookmarks: main main@git main@origin Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46) Adjust config diff --git a/config.py b/config.py index 7366a4e31d..174ffea06b 100644 --- a/config.py +++ b/config.py @@ -1,1 +1,1 @@ -DEFAULT_LIMIT = 10 +DEFAULT_LIMIT = 20

Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Creating & evolving changes

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:

$ @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 849165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

On commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:

jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here.

$ Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set)

jj status shows repo state with diff stats.

$ The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config

jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

$

This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:

$ Commit ID: 66b59f20c534705cfb753c722222290e9185b22c Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:26:43) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:26:43) (no description set) diff --git a/main.py b/main.py new file mode 100644 index 0000000000..c74cd2e0e0 --- /dev/null +++ b/main.py @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ def my_new_feature(): +def my_new_feature(): + pass $ @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:26:43 66b59f20 │ (no description set) ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

$ Working copy (@) now at: kpqxywon 6b89ffb2 Implement the feature Parent commit (@-) : royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this new feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:

$ Working copy (@) now at: nlrtlrxv 6cca2add (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : kpqxywon 6b89ffb2 Implement the feature $ @ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:35:49 6cca2add │ (empty) (no description set) ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

We’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

$ The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : nlrtlrxv 6cca2add (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): kpqxywon 6b89ffb2 Implement the feature

jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj new combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

$ Working copy (@) now at: qmkrwlvp 91067ad0 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv e1b06678 Use the feature $ @ qmkrwlvp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 91067ad0 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678 │ Use the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

To inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:

$ Commit ID: e1b066782aa1a565c1e5d38ef27a308aa58e7e4c Change ID: nlrtlrxvuuskxprvtuznquqzqzzwvnzk Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:41:30) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:41:30) Use the feature diff --git a/main.py b/main.py index c74cd2e0e0..0714ec450b 100644 --- a/main.py +++ b/main.py @@ -1,2 +1,4 @@ def my_new_feature(): def my_new_feature(): pass + +do_something(my_new_feature())

We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

$ Working copy (@) now at: qwyusntz 46a2ffda (empty) Document the feature Parent commit (@-) : kpqxywon 6b89ffb2 Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files

A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj new. Here’s the current commit graph:

$ @ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:46:35 46a2ffda │ (empty) Document the feature │ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

Revsets

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r <REVSET> flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Parent of @:

$ ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~

Grandchildren of r:

$ @ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a │ Document the feature ~ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678 │ Use the feature ~

Commits between r and @, inclusive:

$ @ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a │ Document the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

Commit k and all descendants:

$ @ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a │ Document the feature │ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:

$ @ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a │ Document the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Navigating the commit graph

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:

$ Working copy (@) now at: kpqxywon 6b89ffb2 Implement the feature Parent commit (@-) : royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 1 files

Our working copy once again shows the changes from kpqxywon.

$ Commit ID: 6b89ffb2a250f622a8638145d65fe8c9bb308dbf Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:26:43) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:33:23) Implement the feature diff --git a/main.py b/main.py new file mode 100644 index 0000000000..c74cd2e0e0 --- /dev/null +++ b/main.py @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ def my_new_feature(): +def my_new_feature(): + pass

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:

$ ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5b55579a │ Document the feature │ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

Instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

Automatic rebasing

If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get new commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

$ Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy. ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 7d293f19 │ Document the feature │ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 41a43a84 ├─┘ Use the feature @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 d9f35831 │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Handling conflicts

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

$ Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy. ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b96f8df4 │ Document the feature │ × nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e562bff4 (conflict) ├─┘ Use the feature @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit…

$ Working copy (@) now at: nlrtlrxv e562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Parent commit (@-) : kpqxywon c501c0bd Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict

And inspect main.py.

def my_new_feature(): print("Hello from the new feature!") <<<<<<< conflict 1 of 1 %%%%%%% diff from: kpqxywon d9f35831 "Implement the feature" (parents of rebased revision) \\\\\\\ to: kpqxywon c501c0bd "Implement the feature" (rebase destination) - pass + return 42 +++++++ nlrtlrxv 41a43a84 "Use the feature" (rebased revision) pass do_something(my_new_feature()) >>>>>>> conflict 1 of 1 ends

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:

$ Working copy changes: M main.py Working copy (@) : nlrtlrxv 34f2e2a1 Use the feature Parent commit (@-): kpqxywon c501c0bd Implement the feature Undo and the op log

Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:

$ Undid operation: 35beb0741f17 (2026-11-15 13:08:39) snapshot working copy Restored to operation: f134ca987b59 (2026-11-15 13:07:18) edit commit e562bff4876f3ea76248c3f730e9e74d3e28e8a0 Working copy (@) now at: nlrtlrxv e562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Parent commit (@-) : kpqxywon c501c0bd Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict New conflicts appeared in 1 commits: nlrtlrxv e562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Hint: To resolve the conflicts, start by creating a commit on top of the conflicted commit: jj new nlrtlrxv Then use `jj resolve`, or edit the conflict markers in the file directly. Once the conflicts are resolved, you can inspect the result with `jj diff`. Then run `jj squash` to move the resolution into the conflicted commit.

More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

Squash workflow

Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit:

$ Working copy (@) now at: wqxolloz b878878a (conflict) (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv e562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict $ @ wqxolloz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:11:44 b878878a (conflict) │ (empty) (no description set) × nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e562bff4 (conflict) │ Use the feature ~

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:

$ @ wqxolloz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:14:12 91181aec │ (no description set) × nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e562bff4 (conflict) │ Use the feature ~

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:

$ Working copy (@) now at: vkywoywq f6b548b3 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv 7208deb7 Use the feature Existing conflicts were resolved or abandoned from 1 commits. $ @ vkywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 f6b548b3 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 7208deb7 │ Use the feature ~

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

More commit graph operations

One of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

$ @ vkywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 f6b548b3 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 7208deb7 │ Use the feature │ ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b96f8df4 ├─┘ Document the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Rebase

Let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:

$ Rebased 2 commits to destination. Working copy (@) now at: vkywoywq 0405560c (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv 9920235b Use the feature Added 1 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files $ @ vkywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 0405560c │ (empty) (no description set) ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 9920235b │ Use the feature ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b96f8df4 │ Document the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

Another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:

$ Working copy (@) now at: wxzmtyol be5ca29b (empty) Prepare for the feature Parent commit (@-) : royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 2 files $ @ wxzmtyol ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:23:29 be5ca29b │ (empty) Prepare for the feature │ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 9920235b │ │ Use the feature │ ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b96f8df4 │ │ Document the feature │ ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c501c0bd ├─┘ Implement the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ $ Rebased 3 commits to destination. $ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 cda0de88 │ Use the feature ○ qwyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 ec9de16f │ Document the feature ○ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 722e7268 │ Implement the feature @ wxzmtyol ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:23:29 be5ca29b │ (empty) Prepare for the feature ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~

Bookmarks and Git branches

jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Pushing a new branch

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:

) ) ) | ))) )

Now jj log shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:

$ ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:33:49 push-nlrtlrxvuusk b1284f61 │ Use the feature ~

We’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like <author name>/<change ID>.

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

Updating a branch

To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

Bookmark squash flow

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

First, create a new commit on top of our branch.

$ Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files

Then make our edits.

$ Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

Squash them into the bookmark branch.

$ Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature

We now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them.

$ Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b]

The remote branch now reflects the new changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

Bookmark advance flow

In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the new commit.

$ Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature

Then make our edits.

$ Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : pptrztmx 89027165 (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature $ Working copy (@) now at: wunttkrp 044f2d98 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : pptrztmx 2341ee4a Add a usage example

The bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:

$ @ wunttkrp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 044f2d98 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ pptrztmx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 2341ee4a │ Add a usage example ○ nlrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:43:16 push-nlrtlrxvuusk aeb869ae │ Use the feature ~

There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:

$ Advanced 1 bookmarks to pptrztmx 2341ee4a push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Add a usage example

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

$ Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move forward from aeb869aef99b to 2341ee4aa554] Checking out a remote branch

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:

Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.
